name: Balghami
tagline: Calm as still water, loyal as family, and slow to anger.
share_line: I don't rush, I don't panic, and I don't hold grudges.

free.summary:
In Unani tradition, Water (Balghami) is the mizaj of balgham, phlegm, the cool and moist humour linked with water and winter. If you are Water, you bring a steadiness most people can only envy. You are the friend who stays calm when the car breaks down on the way to a wedding, the sibling who listens without judging, and the person everyone wants beside them in a hospital waiting room.

You are patient, gentle and loyal. You prefer peace to drama and would rather adjust than argue. The flip side is that you can be slow to start, reluctant to change, and too willing to go along with others just to keep the peace.

Physically, Unani texts picture the Water person as soft-bodied and cool to the touch, a deep sleeper with an unhurried digestion and a real dislike of cold weather. Many Water people find they feel lighter, sharper and more energetic with warm, freshly cooked, gently spiced food, regular movement and early, lighter dinners.
traits: Calm under pressure; your steady presence lowers the temperature in any room.
Patient and accepting; you give people time, space and second chances.
Deeply loyal to family and friends, often the quiet glue holding everyone together.
Prefers routine and the familiar; change feels uncomfortable until you've had time to adjust.
Avoids conflict, sometimes swallowing your own needs to keep everyone happy.
Slow to start but steady once going; you finish what others abandon halfway.
body_signs: Unani texts describe a softer, fuller frame that gains weight more easily than it loses it.
Skin tends to be soft, smooth and cool to the touch.
Digestion runs on the slower side; cold or heavy meals can sit for a long time.
Sleep comes easily and runs deep, and mornings can feel slow to get going.
You feel the cold more than most, reach for the heating first, and come alive in warm, dry weather.
Thirst is usually low, so you may forget to drink water even on busy days.
free.quick_tip: Start the day with a cup of warm water or ginger chai with a little honey instead of anything chilled. Unani tradition suggests warmth and gentle spice help a cool, moist mizaj shake off morning heaviness.

premium.deep_dive:
In the Canon, Ibn Sina described balgham as the cool, moist humour that keeps the body lubricated and nourished, a kind of reserve the body can draw on. In a Water (Balghami) person, that reserve is generous. Tradition saw this temperament as the most stable of the four: slow to heat up, slow to dry out, slow to change. That stability is your gift, and stagnation is its shadow.

In the body, Unani tradition associates this mizaj with a softer build, smooth cool skin, deep sleep, low thirst and an unhurried digestion. Cold and damp are your weak points: iced drinks, heavy creamy food, late dinners and long hours of sitting at a desk are traditionally believed to add more cold and moisture than you need. When the balance tips, many Water people notice heaviness, sluggish mornings, a puffy feeling and low motivation. The traditional answer is warmth and lightness: freshly cooked food, gentle spices like ginger and black pepper, a little honey, regular movement and fewer naps.

In the mind, the cool, moist quality gives patience and a good memory. You learn steadily, think things through and rarely make rash decisions. You are often the family member who remembers everyone's birthdays and keeps old friendships alive for decades, across time zones. The challenge is momentum. You may delay decisions until they make themselves, or stay in a job, a city, a routine or a role long after it stopped serving you.

Emotionally, Water people are traditionally described as gentle, contented and peaceful. Anger comes slowly and rarely. Your quiet risk is suppression: going along with the family's plan, an aunty's rishta suggestion or a friend's request, then feeling unheard. Speaking up early, and kindly, is your growth edge.

Across life stages, Unani tradition saw later life as gathering cool moisture, so a young Water person may seem mature beyond their years: calm, homely, steady. The warmth of the busy twenties and thirties can suit you well, lifting your energy and drive. Later in life, keeping active and warm becomes especially important, because tradition holds that coolness and heaviness naturally increase with age.

Across the seasons, winter is your mirror. The tradition linked balgham with cold, wet weather, so grey, damp months and early dark evenings can feel heavy, especially if you live somewhere winter lasts half the year. Spring and early summer are often when you feel lightest and most energetic, as long as you don't cool yourself down with endless iced drinks. Living well as a Water person means adding warmth and movement to a naturally peaceful life.

foods_favour.item: Fresh ginger (adrak) in cooking and chai
foods_favour.why: Warm and lightening; Unani tradition uses it to lift a cool, moist system.
Classically rated warm and dry; a teaspoon in warm water is a traditional Water morning habit.
A warm, light broth that tradition favours on cold, heavy days.

foods_favour.item: Saag, with makki or wholewheat roti
foods_favour.why: Mustard greens are traditionally warm and dry, ideal winter food for you; go light on the butter.
Millet is warm and drying by Unani reckoning, a good winter swap for white bread.
Dry-roasted, they give warmth and crunch without the heaviness of fried snacks.

foods_favour.item: Lean lamb or goat, well spiced
foods_favour.why: Warm and nourishing; best as a shorba or light curry rather than a heavy, rich dish.
Warm and easy to digest; classical Unani texts praise soft-boiled eggs as quick nourishment.
Warm and dry; aloo methi or a pinch of kasuri methi in dal is a traditional answer to heaviness.
Warm winter roots that tradition values for gentle heat and nourishment.
Traditionally warm and dry and thought to lighten heaviness; enjoy it in daytime, not at night.

foods_favour.item: A few dates, walnuts and almonds in winter
foods_favour.why: Warm and nourishing; a small handful adds warmth without a heavy meal.

foods_favour.item: Gur (jaggery) with sesame in small amounts
foods_favour.why: A warmer alternative to white sugar, traditionally enjoyed through the winter months.

foods_favour.item: Moong or masoor dal with a garlic tarka
foods_favour.why: Light dals, warmed with garlic and zeera, balance cool moisture without adding heaviness.

foods_limit.why: Cold on cold; tradition says they slow an already unhurried digestion.
Cold, sweet and creamy: triple trouble for a cool, moist mizaj, especially in winter.
Cool and moist; keep yogurt to daytime meals and in smaller portions.
Rich and moist; they sit heavily and add to sluggishness.
Oil adds moisture and heaviness, especially on rainy or grey days.

foods_limit.item: Large portions of rice at dinner
foods_limit.why: Heavy and filling late in the day; tradition prefers a lighter, earlier dinner for you.
Soft, heavy and often sweet; they tend to leave a Water system slow and full.

foods_limit.item: Cucumber, watermelon and cooling fruit in winter
foods_limit.why: Cool and moist; fine in summer heat, but go easy when it's cold.
Thick, cool and heavy; lighter milk, warmed with a slice of ginger, sits better.
Eating close to bedtime is traditionally believed to add heaviness and slow your mornings.

drinks: Ginger chai with less milk: warming and helps you shake off morning heaviness
Warm water with honey and lemon on waking: a traditional Water wake-up
Kahwa or green tea with cinnamon and cardamom: light, warm and fragrant after meals
Chicken soup in a mug: a warming winter drink and snack in one
Saunf-ajwain water after heavy meals: many people find it settles and lightens
Room-temperature water through the day: you forget to drink, so keep a bottle in sight
spices_herbs: Kali mirch (black pepper): warm and drying; add it to eggs, soups and raita
Adrak and lehsan (ginger and garlic): the foundation of warm, light Water cooking
Darchini (cinnamon): warming in kahwa, chai or porridge on dark mornings
Ajwain (carom seeds): traditionally used to lighten heavy or fried dishes
Kalonji (nigella seeds): warm and dry, lovely sprinkled on roti or dal
Zeera and haldi (cumin and turmeric): everyday warmth for dal and sabzi

daily_routine.morning: Don't snooze. Unani tradition sees oversleeping as adding heaviness to a cool, moist body, so wake around sunrise, or at a fixed early hour when winter mornings are dark, and stay up. Open the curtains, drink warm water, and move for 20 to 30 minutes: a brisk walk, skipping or a few rounds of the stairs. Keep breakfast warm and light: an egg, a roti, or porridge with cinnamon.
daily_routine.midday: Make lunch your main warm meal, freshly cooked and eaten on time. Add salad, but in winter choose radish, onion and carrot over a heap of cucumber. Resist the long post-lunch nap or desk slump; a ten-minute walk or a stretch keeps you from sliding into the afternoon dip.
daily_routine.evening: Evening is a good time for your second dose of movement, even a family walk around the block. Eat a light, early dinner: soup, dal with roti or a lean curry. Skip dessert most nights, or keep it to a small piece of gur with a cup of kahwa or green tea.
daily_routine.sleep: You sleep deeply, so aim for seven to eight hours, not ten. Go to bed on purpose rather than drifting off in front of the TV. Keep your room warm in winter without overheating it, and avoid eating in the two hours before bed so you wake up lighter.

seasons.summer: Summer often suits you better than most, because heat warms a cool system, whether it's a long Gulf summer or a short, bright one up north. Enjoy fruit, lassi and cucumber in sensible amounts, but don't overdo iced drinks or arctic air conditioning. Stay active in the cooler hours, and keep meals light so you don't feel lazy all afternoon.
seasons.rains: Rainy, damp weather adds moisture to your own, so many Water people feel heaviest now, whether it's monsoon back home or weeks of drizzle abroad. Choose warm, freshly cooked food with ginger and black pepper, skip fried snacks, and keep moving indoors on wet days, even just pacing during phone calls.
seasons.winter: Your most challenging season, especially if you live somewhere with long, dark, damp winters. Tradition says balgham rises with cold, wet weather, so you may feel sleepy, heavy and slow. Lean into warming food: saag, eggs, soup, ginger chai, gur and dry fruit. Dress warmly, keep your feet covered, chase daylight when you can, and don't skip exercise just because it's dark early.
seasons.spring: Spring is your fresh start. Many Water people feel lighter and more energetic as the cold lifts. It's a good time to begin a new fitness routine, eat more seasonal greens, and clear out winter's heavy eating habits before the next wedding or festival fills your plate again.

premium.movement: Movement is the single most important habit for a Water person, because tradition sees a cool, moist body as prone to sluggishness. Choose activity that warms you up and gets you gently sweating: brisk walking, cycling, skipping, badminton, or practising the dance for the next family wedding. Morning exercise is especially helpful for shaking off heaviness. Start small and steady, which suits your nature, then build up. A walking partner, a gym buddy or a family badminton game makes it far more likely you'll keep going.
premium.emotional_balance: Unani counts the emotions among the six essential factors of health, and for a Water person the risk is not too much feeling but too much holding in. You keep the peace, absorb other people's moods and quietly carry family tension. Over time this can turn into low motivation or a heavy dil. Practise saying what you want early and simply: 'I'd prefer this', 'I need a day to think'. Try one new thing each month, even a new route home or a short course. If sadness or low energy lasts more than a couple of weeks, talk to a doctor or counsellor. You deserve the same care you give everyone else.
premium.fasting: Many Water people find fasting manageable, because hunger and thirst arrive slowly, whether you keep Ramadan, a vrat, a weekly fast or an intermittent-fasting window. Keep the meal before the fast warm and simple: an egg, a roti or porridge, a few dates and warm water, rather than a heavy paratha with lassi. Break the fast with water and something warm, then lightly spiced food. Go easy on fried snacks and iced drinks, and add a gentle walk afterwards, exactly when you'd otherwise feel heavy.

when_out_of_balance: Hitting snooze again and again, and still feeling heavy after a full night's sleep.
Afternoon slumps that send you looking for a nap or something sweet.
Postponing decisions and tasks until they turn into emergencies.
Feeling puffy, heavy or slow after cold, creamy or late meals.
Saying 'it's fine' to family when it isn't, then feeling quietly resentful.

with_other_mizaj.damvi: A warm, easygoing match. The sociable energy of Air (Damvi) pulls you out of the house, and your calm steadies their busy schedule. You both enjoy food and family, so keep an eye on the shared dinner table. Let them plan the outings, let yourself plan the quiet Sundays, and keep dinners lighter than your love.
with_other_mizaj.safravi: Classic Unani balance: the warmth and dryness of Fire (Safravi) meet your coolness and moisture. They bring urgency, you bring patience. Don't let their quick temper push you into silence; say your piece calmly. In turn, encourage them to rest, and let their energy get you moving on the things you'd otherwise postpone.
with_other_mizaj.balghami: Two Water spouses make a peaceful, loving home with almost no shouting. The risk is that nothing moves: decisions wait, plans stall, and both of you avoid hard conversations. Schedule a monthly planning chat, take turns being the one who pushes, and build movement into shared routines like evening walks.
with_other_mizaj.saudavi: With Earth (Saudavi) you share coolness, which makes for a quiet, serious, loyal home. Your moisture softens their dryness, and their careful planning gives your calm some direction. Watch for both of you withdrawing at once. Make warmth deliberate: shared meals, outings with friends, and asking each other how you really are.
